drills.name: Athletic stance
drills.desc: Ankles, knees, and hips flexed evenly with shins pressing the boot tongues and hands forward in view. Stability comes from stacking the joints so the quads and glutes share the load instead of the lower back. Every other skill in skiing is built on holding this shape while the terrain tries to break it.
mistakes: Sitting back on the tails — quads torch and the skis wander.
Bending at the waist instead of flexing the ankles and knees.
Locked, straight legs that turn every bump into a launch ramp.

drills.name: Skating on flats
drills.desc: Propelling yourself on flat ground with alternating diagonal pushes off the inside edges, gliding on one ski at a time. Drive comes from a lateral hip extension identical to a skater's stride, and the glide phase trains single-leg balance you will use in every turn. It is also the fastest way to warm up cold legs.
mistakes: Pushing straight back instead of out to the side off the edge.
Never committing to the gliding ski, so it becomes a shuffle rather than a skate.

drills.name: Full-run stance endurance
drills.alt: Legs that last to the last lift
drills.desc: Holding the flexed athletic stance through long top-to-bottom runs without straightening up to rest. The limiting factor is quad endurance under constant eccentric load — the muscles brake against gravity for minutes at a time. Skiers who fatigue stand up tall, sit back, and get hurt in the afternoon.
mistakes: Standing bolt upright to rest mid-run and losing the stance when it matters.
Training only short sets — ski runs load the legs for minutes, not seconds.

drills.name: Snowplow (wedge)
drills.alt: The pizza — first speed control and turns
drills.desc: Holding the ski tips together and tails wide, braking on both inside edges and steering by weighting one ski more than the other. The wedge is held by a constant isometric squeeze of the inner thighs, which is why beginners' adductors ache after day one. It teaches the weight-shift logic every later turn reuses.
mistakes: Leaning back when scared — the wedge stops braking and the skis run away.
Crossing the tips by pushing the knees together instead of the tails apart.
Twisting the shoulders to turn instead of pressuring the outside ski.

drills.name: Parallel turns
drills.desc: Steering both skis through the arc simultaneously, with the outside ski carrying most of the pressure and both edges rolling together. The turn is driven by leg rotation under a quiet upper body that keeps facing down the fall line. Committing weight to the outside ski early is the single change that makes parallel click.
mistakes: Rotating the shoulders into the turn instead of turning the legs under a stable torso.
Weight stuck on the inside ski, which skids and stalls the arc.
Popping up tall between turns instead of flowing edge to edge.

drills.name: Pole planting
drills.alt: Timing the turn with the pole touch
drills.desc: A light wrist-flick touch of the downhill pole that marks the trigger point of each new turn. Its value is rhythm and a forward, downhill-facing upper body — the plant pulls your mass over the skis exactly when you need to commit. Done from the wrist, not the whole arm, it stabilizes rather than rotates the torso.
mistakes: Swinging the whole arm across the body, which rotates the shoulders uphill.
Planting late so the pole trails behind instead of triggering the turn.
Dropping the hands after the plant — they belong forward and in view.

drills.name: Short turns
drills.alt: Quick rhythmic turns in a narrow corridor
drills.desc: Fast, linked turns within a corridor a few metres wide, with the legs swinging beneath a torso that never stops facing downhill. The tempo comes from rapid leg rotation and rebound out of each edge set, with a pole plant on every beat. Short turns are the skill that makes steep, narrow terrain feel controlled.
mistakes: Letting the upper body swing with the skis instead of separating hips from torso.
Pivoting flat skis with no edge set, so speed builds turn after turn.
Losing the pole-plant rhythm — the turns immediately fall apart.

drills.name: Side slipping
drills.desc: Sliding sideways down the slope by feathering the uphill edges — flatten to release, roll the knees uphill to grip. All control lives in millimetres of ankle and knee angulation, making this the purest edge-awareness drill in skiing. It is also the practical way down anything too steep to turn on.
mistakes: Leaning the whole body uphill — the edges bite and stop the slide abruptly.
Releasing both edges completely and side-slipping into a downhill slip with no brake.

drills.name: Hockey stop
drills.desc: A rapid pivot of both skis across the fall line followed by a hard edge set that sprays snow and kills speed in a body length. The pivot comes from the legs turning under a countered torso, and the stop from sinking low against the edges as they bite. Owning this stop is what makes real speed feel safe.
mistakes: Leaning uphill into the stop, so the edges wash out and slide.
Pivoting the shoulders first — the skis follow late and the stop drifts.
Staying tall through the edge set instead of dropping the hips to absorb it.

drills.name: Carving
drills.alt: Clean arcs on the edges, no skid
drills.desc: Tipping the skis on edge early and letting the sidecut draw a clean pencil-line arc with no skidding. The load comes through a strong outside leg while the hips move inside the turn, and the obliques hold the angulated shape against forces that can exceed body weight. Speed becomes the reward instead of the enemy.
mistakes: Banking the whole body inside instead of angulating — the edges lose grip mid-turn.
Rushing the top of the turn with a pivot, which turns the carve into a skid.
Letting the inside ski trail flat instead of tipping both skis together.

drills.name: Dynamic carving & angulation
drills.desc: Driving the hips far inside the turn while the upper body stays level over the outside ski, creating the high edge angles racers use. The position is held by massive lateral core and glute strength as g-forces stack up through the belly of the turn. The reward is grip and acceleration out of every arc.
mistakes: Dropping the inside shoulder and banking — grip vanishes exactly at peak load.
Parking on the edge angle instead of building and releasing it progressively.
Letting the outside leg collapse under g-force instead of resisting long and strong.

drills.name: Mogul absorption
drills.desc: Letting the knees fold up toward the chest over each bump and extending into the trough behind it, so the head travels in a level line while the legs piston. The work is heavy eccentric quad loading at high frequency, with the hip flexors actively pulling the feet up. Without absorption, moguls bounce you out of every turn.
mistakes: Stiff legs that launch off every bump instead of folding to swallow it.
Sitting back after two or three bumps, making absorption impossible.
Looking at the mogul under your feet instead of two or three bumps ahead.

drills.name: Jump turns on steeps
drills.alt: Hopping the skis around on steep pitches
drills.desc: On pitches too steep to arc, both skis are unweighted with an explosive hop and pivoted across the fall line in the air, landing on a hard edge set. Power comes from a coiled leg extension off the downhill edge and a decisive pole plant that anchors the rotation. Commitment is the technique — hesitation mid-air is a fall.
mistakes: A timid half-hop that leaves the tails in the snow and twists the knees.
Landing flat-based and accelerating instead of landing on the uphill edges.
Leaning into the hill on landing — the edges slip on the steepest part.

drills.name: Powder technique
drills.desc: Riding a centered stance with even weight on both skis, using a rhythmic bounce to unweight and steer both legs together through the deep snow. Flotation comes from patience and rhythm rather than force — the skis rise and fall like a porpoise instead of being wrestled edge to edge. Sitting back to 'keep tips up' is a myth that only burns the quads.
mistakes: Leaning back — the quads blow up and the skis dive on every extension anyway.
Forcing hard edge sets like on groomed snow instead of steering both skis in rhythm.
Splitting the skis apart, which lets one dive while the other floats.

drills.name: Crud & variable snow
drills.desc: Driving through tracked, chopped, and refrozen snow with a slightly wider stance, strong forward pressure, and a torso braced against unpredictable deflections. The skill is aggression with shock absorption — the legs stay supple while the core refuses to be twisted off line. Timid, backseat skiing gets thrown around; committed skiing planes through.
mistakes: Backing off and getting bucked by every pile — crud rewards commitment.
A narrow stance with no lateral base when the snow grabs a ski.
Letting the hands and eyes drop after the first deflection.
